video.title: The Massive Machine Hidden in the Deep Ocean

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Cold-open mystery: 900 floating spheres strung off Sicily; in 2023 something smaller than an electron tore through at nearly light speed with a signal 30x stronger than ever seen; telescopes worldwide swing to look and find ... 'nothing.' Hook is the opening line; payoff is 'nothing' (63.1). Later starts open on 'them'/'they' pointing back.

Thought experiment: fly to the next star, 40 trillion km, 75,000 years -- 'a lot of space in space'; shrink to a fundamental particle and atoms of solid rock are as empty as space between stars. Payoff: 'That is what it's like to be a neutrino.' Starts right after the AT&T sponsor line.

Explanation: catch a neutrino and you can trace exactly where it came from and see inside what made it; like a doctor switching from visible light to X-rays to see bones. Payoff: 'catching neutrinos is like developing X-ray vision for our universe.' Earlier start needs the on-screen 'this one' comparison of three options.

Explanation: a neutrino hits a proton, making a particle that flies through water faster than light; nothing beats light in vacuum, but light slows in water; Cleo asks 'is it like a sonic boom?' and the scientist says exactly -- instead of a boom, a flash of blue light. Speakers inferred from text. Payoff 625.3; 'That is what these sensors can see' (627.6) acceptable.

Discovery story: in 2017 a neutrino set off IceCube, telescopes swung to a blazar 4 billion light years away, and only the neutrino confirmed it as a cosmic engine, the source of the heavy metals in us. Earliest landing 818.0; 'and a source of cosmic rays' (820.6) and 'the beginning of a whole new era in astronomy' (833.4) are both acceptable longer ends.

In 2022 IceCube found an active galaxy 50 million light years away whose core is hidden by gas and dust; light couldn't escape, 'but neutrinos could, and did' -- the first look inside a cosmic engine light could never show us (869.8).

also_ok.why: Neutrinos are the 'ghost particle': they pass through stars, planets, walls, you -- a hundred trillion through your body every second; hold up your thumb. Strong fact but short (~22s) and opens on 'these particles'.
Every ~10 seconds a star goes supernova; the iron in your blood traces back to one; light can't get out of the core fast, so 'neutrinos are your messenger.' Opens past 'So, for example,'.

Question and punchline: if neutrinos pass through everything they pass through detectors too -- how do you study something that never interacts with you? 'You build a very, very big and very crazy machine.' Lands as a line, explains nothing.

A neutrino's life told as a story: born in a supernova, a dull billion years in a straight line, then by chance it runs headfirst into some poor proton off Sicily -- unlikely, but a hundred trillion per second means some will.
Closing reflection: what the effort says about us -- a former factory worker proud to build it; 'what are the machines we build, if not extensions of ourselves.' Speakers inferred.

negatives.why: Three ways we study space; 'this one gets blocked ... this one gets tossed around' leans on on-screen graphics.
Building a DOM by hand, 'sign it', 'he's checking my work' -- narration of what is on screen.
Single-photon sensitivity and 'why are we trying to detect light? ... Wait, what?' -- the answer comes minutes later.
'Think about it as a giant telescope where the lens is the entire Earth' -- quotable, but the support (only looking at particles through the Earth) came just before.
'This is what KM3net sees, and this is what IceCube sees' -- chart read aloud.
'Just look at this, nearly a thousand scientists on this paper' -- screen narration.
